bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **GE engine dependency** — single biggest risk; deliveries repeatedly slipped (FY26 commitment of 2/month did not materialise). FY27 plan rests on ~20 engines arriving (1 in June, 2/month from Aug). Casting/supply-chain issues at GE Tier-2/3.
- **LCA software/testing refinements** — mgmt vague; analysts (JPMorgan) flagged investor anxiety that even FY27 deliveries are at risk. CMD repeatedly deflected specifics ("more technicalities").
- **Lumpy delivery-based revenue recognition** → quarterly volatility.
- **Manpower/private-sector competition** for skilled labour as 5-6 programs run in parallel (FY28-29).
- **Global supply-chain "slowness"** beyond GE (Honeywell now stabilised; radars/components).
- **GE penalty** for delayed engines — exists per contract but mgmt declined to quantify ("let delivery happen, then we'll see").
- **Uttam radar** integration controlled by DRDO — not in the 83-program; planned for the 97-program only.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: New CMD Ravi Kota (since 1 May 2026); measured, candid on supply chain but deliberately evasive on LCA technical/software specifics and GE penalty quantum. CFO Senapati precise on numbers and margin mechanics. Overall tone: confident-but-hedged ("plan B," "ways and means"); credibility partly hostage to whether the oft-slipped Aug/Sep LCA start finally holds.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- Manufacturing already grew via ALH/AL-31FP/RD-33 — LCA is incremental upside, not the base; the "20 LCA" target may concentrate in H2FY27, risking spill into FY28.
- ~INR8,000-8,100 cr of inventory is locked in undelivered LCA (raw material + WIP); unbilled revenue is on already-delivered units stuck on documentation — a quiet working-capital / cash-conversion drag.
- ROH (the higher-margin, ~62% pool) is structurally flat until LCA/LCH enter overhaul (~3 yrs post-delivery) — near-term growth is lower-margin manufacturing-led.
- The 97 LCA order is what guarantees ~100% capacity utilisation across all 3 lines — backlog underwrites the capex.
- Safran LEAP + SJ-100 + SSLV = optionality to diversify beyond captive Indian-MoD demand into global civil/space supply chains.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Integrated aerospace business spanning R&D, production and MRO including PBL solutions for fixed-wing aircraft, rotary-wing aircraft, aero-engines, LRUs and airborne systems (SWOT - Strengths)
- Strong order book ensuring long-term revenue visibility (SWOT - Strengths); management states the order book provides 7-8 years of revenue visibility
- Expertise in aircraft upgrade for Defence customers including re-engining, avionics upgrade and weapon system integration (SWOT - Strengths)
- Expertise in executing Transfer of Technology (ToT) projects - has absorbed ToT and produced MiG-21, MiG-27, Su-30MKI, Jaguar, Hawk, Dornier-228 and AVRO (SWOT - Strengths)
- Design and development expertise across a wide helicopter range - ALH variants, LCH, LUH in the 3.5-to-5.5-ton class, civil ALH Dhruv-NG, and IMRH/DBMRH under development in the 10-15-ton class (SWOT - Strengths)
- Trusted partner of the Indian Defence Forces for supporting ageing fleets, some more than 60 years old (SWOT - Strengths)
- Government ownership and Maharatna PSU status - President of India through MoD holds 71.64% equity
- Policy tailwind: Atmanirbhar Bharat, Positive Indigenisation List and export promotion measures cited as opportunities
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Dependence on foreign OEMs for critical components, spares, materials and LRUs — Flagged by management twice - as the first item under MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' ('Dependence on foreign OEMs for supply of critical components and Spares') and as the first SWOT weakness ('Dependency on foreign OEMs for critical materials and LRUs'). It is structural, not cyclical: the annual report's own materials-consumption disclosure shows imported raw materials, spare parts and components at 80% of total consumption in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 77%), i.e. import reliance INCREASED during the year even as indigenisation was the stated top strategy. Management also concedes 'engine supply issues observed in prior periods'. Mitigations disclosed: accelerated R&D, technology-transfer partnerships including higher localisation in engines, vendor development programmes, diversification of suppliers, development of alternate indigenous sources, strategic inventories for critical items, an MoU with MIDHANI for a strategic metal bank for critical raw materials, and a stated aim of 65-75%+ indigenisation for major platforms. [The 80%/77% figures are ratios from a financial-statement note that this extraction otherwise does not reproduce; no rupee amounts are carried.]
- Customer concentration - the business is effectively a single-buyer business dependent on the Ministry of Defence — MD&A lists 'Dependence on limited customers for new contracts' among major risks and states under SWOT Threats: 'Mainly dependent on MoD for the contracts. Any change in procurement policy / preference can adversely affect our ability to grow or maintain our sales, earnings and cash flow.' The BRSR confirms the Indian Air Force, Navy, Army and Coast Guard as primary customers. The same counterparty is also the controlling shareholder (President of India through MoD, 71.64%), so commercial and ownership concentration coincide. A specific named vector is a shift 'from nomination to competitive procurement' by regular customers, which would remove the single-tender/nomination basis on which much of HAL's work is placed.
- Execution risk on complex indigenous programmes - timelines, integration and certification — MD&A: 'Challenges in meeting aggressive timelines for complex indigenous platforms, integration issues, and certification requirements', reinforced by the SWOT weakness 'Long gestation periods and complexities in project execution'. This is the risk that sits directly against the forward promises - a 24+ aircraft/year LCA Mk1A rate, expedited HTT-40 production, and the IMRH / LCA Mk2 / CATS / HLFT / UAV development pipeline. It is corroborated inside the accounts: the inventory turnover ratio fell during FY 2025-26 because of rising work-in-progress on LCA Mk1A, HTT-40, ALH, LCH, Su-30 and AL-31FP engines - i.e. capital is accumulating in unfinished programmes. Mitigation disclosed: additional assembly lines to de-risk execution (a 3rd LCA Mk1A line was established at Nasik) and capacity/infrastructure build-up.
- Erosion of the nomination monopoly by private Indian players partnered with global OEMs, and by foreign entrants — SWOT Threats name 'Collaborations of Indian Private Companies with Global OEMs and capability building by their entities' and 'Direct competition from foreign companies entering into Indian market and pricing pressures in international markets'; MD&A Risks repeats 'Competition from domestic and foreign players'. MD&A industry commentary itself records 'greater private sector participation in the defence ecosystem' as a key structural shift - so the same Atmanirbhar policy that expands HAL's addressable market also builds its future competitors. The Outlook section concedes 'increasing competition both from private sector and global players' as a challenge to the positive outlook.
- Technological obsolescence and the pace of upgrade required across a very long-lived fleet — MD&A Risks: 'Rapid advancements leading to obsolescence of existing systems'; SWOT Threats: 'Rapid technological disruptions requiring continuous upgradation'; Outlook: 'evolving technological requirements'. The exposure is amplified by the nature of the installed base HAL supports - it describes itself as a 'trusted partner of Indian Defence Forces for providing support to aging fleets, some of which are more than 60 years old'. Mitigation disclosed: investment in R&D, advanced materials, advanced manufacturing technologies, automation, Industry 4.0, additive manufacturing, digitalisation and AI-enabled systems.
- Supply-chain disruption from geopolitical events, including Russia-origin supply exposure — SWOT Threats: 'Supply chain disruptions due to geopolitical issues'; Outlook: 'supply chain constraints'. HAL's MiG Complex is built around production, MRO and upgrade of fixed-wing aircraft and engines 'mainly of Russian origin', and a financial-statement note records bulk contracts with the Russian Federation under which suppliers do not indicate itemised prices, so the value of materials issued has to be assessed on technical estimates and remains subject to adjustment at the end of the project - a disclosed weakness in price transparency on a geopolitically exposed supply line. Mitigations: supplier diversification, alternate indigenous sources, strategic inventories and closer coordination with global suppliers.
- Governance capacity risk - Board and statutory committees ran part of the year without valid constitution — The Board's Report states that due to non-appointment of the requisite number of Independent Directors, the Audit Committee and the Nomination & Remuneration Committee 'were not in valid constitution during the financial year till June 1, 2025', and that the CSR & Sustainable Development Committee, the Stakeholders Relationship Committee AND the Risk Management Committee were 'also not in valid constitution during the period from April 28, 2025 till June 1, 2025' - i.e. all five statutory committees, including the very committee that owns ESG, cyber security and business continuity risk, lapsed simultaneously for over a month. As on March 31, 2026 five Independent Director positions including the one woman Independent Director were still vacant against a sanctioned strength of seven. A disclosed consequence: related-party transactions requiring Audit Committee recommendation between April 1 and June 1, 2025 were put directly to the Board. HAL cannot self-remedy this - all directors are appointed by the President of India through the Administrative Ministry.
- Export weakness - exports are a rounding error in turnover despite being a stated strategic priority — SWOT weakness: 'Limited presence in high-value global export markets'. The BRSR quantifies it: exports contributed 1.58% of total turnover in FY 2025-26, to 13 countries during the year (30 countries over the Company's history). Expanding exports is one of HAL's stated principal strategies and the outlook leans on 'intensifying efforts to expand its global footprint', so the gap between the strategic weight placed on exports and their current contribution is itself the risk - domestic MoD demand remains effectively the only revenue engine, which loops back to the customer-concentration risk above.

business.body: HAL designs, develops, manufactures, repairs, overhauls, upgrades and services a wide range of products including aircraft, helicopters, aero-engines, avionics, accessories and aerospace structures. The Company was set up to meet the requirement of the Indian Defence Forces - the Indian Air Force, Indian Army, Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard - in the area of aerospace, and also supports civil and international customers. It relies on indigenous research as well as technology-transfer and licence agreements to manufacture its products, and its operations are organised into five complexes covering production, MRO, upgrade and R&D.

outlook.body:
- Enhance indigenisation content in HAL's products (stated first principal strategy in MD&A 'Our Strategies')
- Enhance export sales, and open export offices in target geographies to explore global markets and export opportunities
- Expand production capabilities to meet growing demand
- Enhance customer satisfaction and improve quality of products and services
- Invest in R&D and adopt advanced manufacturing technologies
- Progress design and development programmes with initial company funding for the Indian Defence Services (i.e. self-funded D&D ahead of a customer order)
- Increase operational efficiency by adopting Industry 4.0, automation and additive manufacturing
- Indigenisation and technology initiatives: accelerated R&D, technology-transfer partnerships (e.g. higher localisation in engines) and vendor development programmes to reduce import dependence
- Supply-chain de-risking: diversify suppliers, develop alternate indigenous sources, coordinate closely with global suppliers (including resolution of engine supply issues observed in prior periods), and build strategic inventories for critical items
- Capacity and infrastructure build-up: significant capex in new production facilities, modernisation of existing lines and establishment of additional assembly lines to de-risk execution
- Dedicated marketing efforts and government-supported export initiatives, with market-oriented products and technology developments to expand in commercial and export markets
- Enhanced digitalisation and IT & AI enabled systems for speedy communication and decision-making
- Use of advanced materials, advanced manufacturing technologies and automation to improve product quality and operational efficiency
- Customer orientation programme: Indian Army-HAL 'Vayu' portal integrating Army and HAL ERP databases, full-scale supply-chain digitisation, dedicated RMSO management teams at every division, and senior-management visits to customer bases/commands
- Expand the global footprint through exports and strategic collaborations with international partners, and pursue emerging opportunities in unmanned systems, advanced materials, digital manufacturing and space applications
- The annual report's stated capital-allocation philosophy for dividend is COMPLIANCE-DRIVEN rather than discretionary: HAL has formulated a Dividend Distribution Policy in terms of Regulation 43A of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 and the Guidelines of the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM), and the final dividend for FY 2025-26 was recommended expressly 'to comply with the Guidelines of DIPAM on capital restructuring with respect to payment of minimum dividend' - i.e. the payout floor is set by the Government's CPSE capital-restructuring rules, not by an internally chosen payout ratio. The policy document is hosted on the Company's website. For FY 2025-26 an interim dividend was declared and paid and a final dividend recommended, and confirmation of the interim dividend and declaration of the final dividend is Ordinary Business item 2 at the 63rd AGM (per-share figures are recorded in the profile and strategy_outlook bundles; the quantum is deliberately not repeated here, and the schema asks for policy intent rather than figures). On the balance sheet side the stated posture is zero leverage - short-term and long-term borrowings were Nil as on March 31, 2026 - with reinvestment routed through dedicated reserves, the Company having transferred amounts during the year to a Research & Development Reserve, an Indigenisation Fund Reserve and the General Reserve, which is a deliberate ring-fencing of internal accruals for indigenisation and R&D. Reinvestment intent is otherwise expressed as capital expenditure on infrastructure and R&D programmes and as self-funded design-and-development ('Progress Design and Development programs with initial company funding for Indian Defence Services'). IMPORTANT: the '=== DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY ===' block routed to this bundle does NOT contain the Dividend Distribution Policy - it contains Note 49 clauses 14.11 to 17A of the standalone financial statements. The policy text itself was never delivered, so the description above is assembled from the Board's Report and the AGM notice, and no payout ratio, dividend formula or reserve-retention rule from the actual policy could be read.
- Occupational health and safety: HAL operates an Occupational Health & Safety Management System (OHMS) aligned with ISO 45001:2018 standards, implemented across all divisions, covering manufacturing, maintenance and support functions and extending to employees, contract workers and trainees; the framework is institutionalised with established processes, certification and governance mechanisms, monitored through defined action plans, audits, training and compliance mechanisms.
- Hazard identification: a Safety Directory maps all operational areas and identifies hazardous activities across mechanical, electrical, chemical, ergonomic and fire hazards plus process- and equipment-specific risks; risk assessment is carried out through Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA), with internal and periodic surveillance audits, shop-floor monitoring and Plant Safety Committee meetings held with equal participation of workers and management.
- Safety performance FY 2025-26 (with FY 2024-25 comparatives): LTIFR per one million person-hours worked - Employees 0.19 (PY 0.17), Workers 0.24 (PY 0.20), i.e. injury frequency ROSE year on year for both categories. Total recordable work-related injuries - Employees 15 (PY 12), Workers 15 (PY 11), also up. Fatalities - Employees 0 (PY: printed '-', a stated nil), Workers 0 (PY 1). High-consequence work-related injury or ill-health excluding fatalities - Employees 0 (PY '-', stated nil), Workers 0 (PY 2). So FY26 was a zero-fatality, zero-high-consequence year that nonetheless saw more recordable injuries and a higher injury frequency rate than FY25. Note the entity's own definition caveat: numbers reported against 'Employees' are total incidents covering all officers, workmen and contract labour.
- A contract labourer, Mr Durgesh Gupta of M/s Bharuka Constructions Pvt. Ltd., died while working in the clean room facility at the new production building at HAL Aerospace Composite Division; a monetary penalty of Rs 30,000 was imposed by the XXIX Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Mayo Hall, Bangalore under NGRBC Principles 3 & 4, and no appeal was preferred. This is the only monetary fine/penalty disclosed for the year; settlement and compounding-fee rows are printed '-' (stated nil), and the non-monetary imprisonment and punishment rows are likewise '-' (stated nil).
- Health and safety governance and infrastructure: workers have established processes to report work-related hazards and remove themselves from unsafe conditions, with complaint registers on the shop floor and Safety Officers appointed under the Factories Act, 1948 / Labour Code; measures include safety audits and inspections, LED awareness screens and signage, toolbox talks, mock drills and fire safety exercises, well-equipped Occupational Health Centres with dedicated ambulances under a medical practitioner, periodical medical examinations, SOPs and work permits for hazardous activities, best-in-class PPE, hazardous and non-hazardous waste removal and disposal, fire alarm and fire hydrant systems in all hangars, daily walk-through surveys, testing of tools, tackles and pressure vessels by competent persons, and continuous monitoring of noise, illumination, ventilation, air quality and ergonomics. Employees and workers also have access to non-occupational healthcare through an in-house dispensary and empanelled multi/super-speciality hospitals.
- Corrective actions disclosed for safety: HIRA in each department with mitigation plans, safety walks/audits and accident investigations, PPE awareness and PPE assessment, safety training programmes, work instructions and safe work practices published on the intranet, electrical safety audit and arc flash assessment, Log Out & Tag Out (LO&TO) implementation, evaluation of building stability, safety barricades for electrical panels, and provisioning of emergency exit stairs in the Commission building.
- Assessment coverage: 100% of HAL's plants and offices were assessed (by the entity, statutory authorities or third parties) for both health and safety practices and working conditions in FY 2025-26.
- Employee/worker complaints on working conditions and on health & safety were both NIL filed and NIL pending in FY 2025-26; the FY 2024-25 comparative shows 2 working-conditions complaints filed and 2 still pending at year end, while the FY25 health & safety row is printed '-' (stated nil). The prior year's 2 pending working-conditions complaints are not shown as carried forward or resolved.
- Unionisation is near-universal and is a durable structural feature of the workforce: 94.04% of permanent employees (20,168 of 21,444) and 92.87% of permanent workers (13,115 of 14,122) are members of associations or unions recognised by the entity in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 95.06% and 95.11%). Both the headcount and the unionised share fell year on year. An appeal route to the CEO/Director 'through the Recognized Union' is a formal stage of the workmen's grievance procedure.
- Grievance redressal is formalised in tiers: for workmen, Section Head then Department Head then Grievance Redressal Committee, with a further petition to the General Manager and a final appeal to the CEO/Director through the recognised union; for officers up to Grade VI, Department Head then Grievance Redressal Committee with the General Manager communicating the decision, and in exceptional cases a final and binding appeal to the CEO/Director.
- Training reach FY 2025-26: 74.19% of employees (15,910 of 21,444) and 77.15% of workers (10,895 of 14,122) received training on health and safety measures, up from 67.72% and 69.86% in FY 2024-25; skill-upgradation training reached 44.78% of employees (up from 37.07%) and 57.20% of workers (up from 55.54%). Female coverage exceeds or matches male coverage in every category, with female workers at 77.50% on skill upgradation versus 55.14% for male workers.
- Performance and career development reviews FY 2025-26: 79.98% of the employee (officer) population covered (5,866 of 7,334), down from 86.96% in FY 2024-25. The Company footnotes that column (A) refers to Performance Appraisal Reports raised during the year rather than headcount, that 2 probationary PARs were raised for officers under probation, and that a Performance Review Board moderates annual PARs. For WORKERS the review columns are blank in both years - only the total workforce counts are printed - so worker coverage is UNKNOWN, not zero; the accompanying note says workers covered under the non-executive Performance Appraisal System have annual and probationary reports raised, except where service in the assessment year is under 3 months.
- Workforce diversity and stability (BRSR Section A, cross-referenced): 23,502 total employees of whom 9.38% are female, and 16,171 total workers of whom 8.98% are female; 583 differently-abled employees and 434 differently-abled workers. Attrition is extremely low - permanent employee turnover 0.23 in FY 2025-26 (0.25 in FY 2024-25, 0.26 in FY 2023-24) and permanent worker turnover 0.04 (0.05, 0.11). Female permanent-worker turnover is printed as an en-dash for FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24, i.e. a stated nil.
- CSR: HAL spent Rs 18,099 Lakh under CSR in FY 2025-26 against a CSR budget/obligation of Rs 16,867 Lakh - an overspend against obligation. Thrust areas are Health Care, Education, Skill Development, Women Empowerment, Rural Development and Promotion of Sports, with projects aligned to Schedule VII of the Companies Act and DPE Guidelines. CSR is applicable under Section 135. A CSR & Sustainable Development Committee is one of the five statutory Board committees, though it was not in valid constitution from April 28, 2025 to June 1, 2025.
- ESG governance: the Company has a Board-approved Risk Management Policy aimed at elimination or reduction of risk exposures through identification and analysis of risks and timely mitigation, and has constituted a Risk Management Committee under Regulation 21 of SEBI LODR whose remit explicitly includes Financial, Operational, ESG, Cyber Security and Business Continuity Plan risks. The BRSR is prepared under Regulation 34(2)(f) on a STANDALONE basis, assured by Sustainability Actions Private Limited, Gurgaon, with REASONABLE ASSURANCE obtained on the BRSR Core.
- Stakeholder engagement: key stakeholder groups are identified through a structured, continuous process mapping customers, employees, shareholders, vendors, regulatory authorities, industry and academic partners, joint ventures, auditors, bankers, collaborators, subsidiaries, all community members within the vicinity of each Division, and Government agencies, with inputs gathered through meetings, consultations, performance reviews, surveys, audits, statutory compliance interactions and CSR engagements, and groups periodically reviewed and prioritised.
- Environment-linked capex and R&D: 0.48% of total capex in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 0.25%) went to technologies improving environmental and social impacts - energy-efficient transformers, HVAC equipment, LED lighting and energy monitoring systems - while the equivalent R&D share is explicitly reported as 'Not tracked' in both years. Environment-linked measures named in the safety section include changing hangar lights from HPMV to LED and constructing rainwater harvesting in Divisions. HAL also leases electric cars from Convergence Energy Services Limited (CESL) over a 5-year term, recognised as right-of-use assets. [Capex percentages and the CESL lease are back-filled from the capex_expansion and profile bundles respectively.]
- Sustainable sourcing: sustainability aspects to be complied with by supply-chain partners are stipulated in tender documents and purchase orders, and in FY 2025-26 the Company sourced 75% of inputs by value through vendors who declared adopting sustainable processes; the balance 25% is sourced from business units whose reports are not in the public domain (sentence truncated in the source). [Back-filled from the capex_expansion bundle.]
- Ethics and anti-corruption: the Company has a Code of Conduct forming part of its Service Rules and a Whistle Blower Policy allowing employees to report unethical practices and suspected fraud to the Chairman of the Audit Committee / Director (HR) / Head of Systems Audit; integrity pacts are signed with vendors for procurements of Rs 5 Crore and above; an independent Vigilance Department headed by a Chief Vigilance Officer is in place. ZERO directors, KMPs, employees or workers faced disciplinary action for bribery/corruption charges in FY 2025-26 or FY 2024-25, and ZERO conflict-of-interest complaints were received in relation to Directors or KMPs in either year - all stated nils, not blanks. [Back-filled from the capex_expansion bundle, which carried BRSR Principle 1.]
- MATERIAL ESG DISCLOSURE ABSENCE - and it is a legal exemption, not an oversight: as a defence Central Public Sector Enterprise, HAL is EXEMPTED from disclosing information on conservation of energy, technology absorption, and foreign exchange earnings and outgo under Section 134(3)(m) read with Rule 8(3) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, vide Notification GSR No. 680(E) dated September 4, 2015. There is therefore no energy-conservation or technology-absorption disclosure anywhere in the Board's Report. Combined with the truncation of the BRSR before Principle 6, this means NO environmental data at all - no energy consumption, no emissions (Scope 1/2/3), no water withdrawal or discharge, no waste generation, no air-emission figures - is available from the routed text. There is no disclosed net-zero, emissions-reduction, renewable-energy or water target of any kind in what was delivered. An analyst should treat HAL's environmental profile as UNDISCLOSED here rather than as absent from the annual report itself.
- Also exempted: formal annual Board evaluation (Gazette Notification GSR 463(E) dated June 5, 2015), and the framing of a Policy on Directors' appointment and remuneration under Section 134(3)(e); SEBI has additionally granted a specific exemption on the NRC's terms of reference for recommending a directors' remuneration policy. In substitution, Independent Directors evaluate the Functional Directors and the Board as a whole in their meeting, and the Board evaluates the Independent Directors without them present. Government Nominee Directors receive no remuneration or sitting fees; Independent Directors receive sitting fees only; Functional Director pay is set by the Government of India and KMP/Senior Management pay scales are governed by Presidential Directives from the Ministry of Defence.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: HAL's stated expansion posture for FY 2025-26 is capacity build-up in support of platform ramp-up rather than entry into new capacity classes. The Board's Report records capital expenditure incurred in FY 2025-26 channelised mainly towards the Green Field Helicopter Project at Tumakuru, augmentation of facilities for LCA, ROH (repair and overhaul) of Su-30, ROH of the AL-31FP engine and IT infrastructure, besides regular replacement and rationalisation of existing facilities on the infrastructure front; on the R&D front the spend went to the IMRH, CATS, UHM, Civil ALH and LUH projects. No commissioning, completion or ramp date is disclosed for any of these projects. The single completed physical expansion named for the year is a 3rd LCA Mk1A production line established at HAL Nasik to enhance LCA Mk1A production capacity. MD&A frames the forward plan as 'Expanding production capabilities to meet growing demand' and, under measures to tackle risks, as 'Capacity and Infrastructure Build-up: significant CAPEX investments in new production facilities, modernization of existing lines and establishment of additional assembly lines to de-risk execution'; the Outlook section attributes expected growth to better supply chain stabilisation, capacity expansion including significant infrastructure investments, and faster production ramp-up for key platforms, with a stated aim of 24+ LCA Mk1A aircraft annually in coming years and expedited HTT-40 production. Organisationally the footprint is 20 Divisions and 10 R&D Centres at ten geographic locations in seven states, grouped into five Complexes (Bangalore, MiG, Helicopter, Accessories, Design). Three supply-chain/industrial build-out agreements signed during the year are relevant to future capacity but reached this bundle only via the sibling strategy_outlook bundle (this bundle's Board's Report copy is truncated before them): an MoU with Yantra India Limited dated September 23, 2025 for funding the establishment of a 10,000 Ton extrusion press; an MoU with Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI) dated November 3, 2025 to set up a strategic metal bank for critical raw materials at MIDHANI; and an agreement with Safran Aircraft Engines dated June 19, 2025 for industrialisation and production of rotating parts for LEAP engines. On the land/asset side, Note 49 clause 14 discloses a large but partly encumbered land estate: Facilities Management Division holds 2,117.289 acres (2,096.189 acres freehold at Bangalore, 15.1 acres at Bagalkot, 6 acres leasehold at Harapanahalli), of which 17.737 acres is under litigation/encroachment by third parties and 10.152 acres is under dispute with BEML; titles to 30 survey numbers totalling 76.475 acres at FMD are not in the Company's name (Records of Tenancy Certificate available); Nasik division freehold land is 4,620.13 acres with 0.0516 acres encroached by 9 persons; about 50.21 acres at Koraput division is encroached by nearby villagers for cultivation; and title deeds are not in the Company's name for land acquired through Government grants in Uttar Pradesh (376.76 acres acquired by the State Government plus 54.30 acres transferred from the IAF in 1973, out of a total 431.06 acres of which 2.03 acres was sold to NHAI). A monetisation exercise for 2.925 acres at Okalipuram, Bengaluru is in process at a Reserve Price of Rs 9,780 lakhs after an earlier e-auction sale was annulled on 4th July 2023 following a Government Audit enquiry. Land has also been given on lease by Korwa Division (39.79 acres to Ordnance Factory Board, 0.115 acres to RCMA, 0.37 acres to AFLE, 3.08 acres to DAV College Trust) and 2.47 acres at Ojhar Nasik to MSRTC, and small parcels have been compulsorily acquired for the Bangalore metro rail project (0.078 acres at Benniganahalli; 711.22 sq m at the Corporate office, with compensation litigation pending before the City Civil Court and Writ Petition No. 640 of 2026 before the High Court). BRSR Principle 2 states that 0.48% of total capex in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 0.25%) was invested in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts - energy-efficient transformers, HVAC equipment, LED lighting and energy monitoring systems - while the equivalent share of R&D expenditure is explicitly 'Not tracked'.

outlook.body:
- The aerospace and defence sector is undergoing a significant structural shift driven by evolving geopolitical dynamics, rapid technological advancements and increasing emphasis on self-reliance, and witnessed sustained momentum during FY 2025-26
- Government focus on 'Atmanirbhar Bharat', indigenisation and modernisation of the Armed Forces supports demand
- Geopolitical uncertainties and the need to enhance operational readiness drove higher demand for indigenous platforms including fighter aircraft, helicopters, engines and related systems
- Structural shifts include greater private sector participation in the defence ecosystem, policy support through positive indigenisation lists, export promotion measures and infrastructure development for aerospace manufacturing
- The industry as a whole saw record-level order inflows and production ramp-ups in select segments
- Outlook for FY 2026-27 and beyond will remain positive, supported by a strong order book providing 7-8 years of revenue visibility
- Management expects improved growth through better supply chain stabilisation, capacity expansion (including significant infrastructure investments) and faster production ramp-up for key platforms
- Execution of ongoing programmes, coupled with anticipated new orders in fighter aircraft, rotary-wing platforms and upgrade projects, is expected to provide revenue visibility over the medium to long term
- Emerging opportunities in unmanned systems, advanced materials, digital manufacturing and space applications are expected to open new growth avenues
- Opportunity set cited: Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan and Positive Indigenisation List; Government focus on building an A&D ecosystem to cut the import bill and make India an A&D hub; civil MRO opportunities in India and expansion in MRO and lifecycle support services; new potential markets in India such as regional jets and UAVs
- Headwinds cited: evolving technological requirements, supply chain constraints, and increasing competition from both private sector and global players; pricing pressure in international markets; possible customer shift from nomination to competitive procurement; dependence on MoD for contracts
- Weaknesses cited: dependency on foreign OEMs for critical materials and LRUs, long gestation periods and complexity in project execution, and limited presence in high-value global export markets
- Mitigation stated: focus on enhancing operational efficiency, strengthening the supply chain ecosystem, accelerating indigenisation and investing in R&D is expected to mitigate these risks
- NOTE: no segment-wise or product-wise performance narrative is provided. MD&A item 5 states Government companies engaged in Defence Production are exempted from Ind AS 108 'Operating Segment' by MCA Notification No. 1/2/2014-CL-V dated February 23, 2018, with disclosure made at Clause 37 of Note 49. This is an explicitly stated absence.
- The Order Book position of the Company stands at Rs 2,54,53,848 Lakh as on March 31, 2026 (Board's Report, 'Order Book Position'). Source unit as printed: ` in Lakh.
- During FY 2025-26 the Company received manufacturing contracts of over Rs 69,60,000 Lakh and ROH (repair and overhaul) contracts of over Rs 17,30,000 Lakh
- Major orders bagged during the year: Qty 97 LCA Mk1A, Qty 06 ALH MkIII MR and Qty 8 Do-228 to the Indian Armed Forces; Qty 10 ALH Dhruv NG to M/s Pawan Hans Ltd; Qty 2 Hindustan-228 to Guyana
- MD&A SWOT lists 'Strong order book ensuring long-term revenue visibility' as a company strength
- MD&A Outlook: the order book provides 7-8 years of revenue visibility, and anticipated new orders in fighter aircraft, rotary-wing platforms and upgrade projects are expected to extend revenue visibility over the medium to long term
- MD&A industry commentary notes the industry as a whole saw record-level order inflows during FY 2025-26

risks.note: Flagged by management twice - as the first item under MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' ('Dependence on foreign OEMs for supply of critical components and Spares') and as the first SWOT weakness ('Dependency on foreign OEMs for critical materials and LRUs'). It is structural, not cyclical: the annual report's own materials-consumption disclosure shows imported raw materials, spare parts and components at 80% of total consumption in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 77%), i.e. import reliance INCREASED during the year even as indigenisation was the stated top strategy. Management also concedes 'engine supply issues observed in prior periods'. Mitigations disclosed: accelerated R&D, technology-transfer partnerships including higher localisation in engines, vendor development programmes, diversification of suppliers, development of alternate indigenous sources, strategic inventories for critical items, an MoU with MIDHANI for a strategic metal bank for critical raw materials, and a stated aim of 65-75%+ indigenisation for major platforms. [The 80%/77% figures are ratios from a financial-statement note that this extraction otherwise does not reproduce; no rupee amounts are carried.]
risks.risk: Dependence on foreign OEMs for critical components, spares, materials and LRUs

risks.note: MD&A lists 'Dependence on limited customers for new contracts' among major risks and states under SWOT Threats: 'Mainly dependent on MoD for the contracts. Any change in procurement policy / preference can adversely affect our ability to grow or maintain our sales, earnings and cash flow.' The BRSR confirms the Indian Air Force, Navy, Army and Coast Guard as primary customers. The same counterparty is also the controlling shareholder (President of India through MoD, 71.64%), so commercial and ownership concentration coincide. A specific named vector is a shift 'from nomination to competitive procurement' by regular customers, which would remove the single-tender/nomination basis on which much of HAL's work is placed.
risks.risk: Customer concentration - the business is effectively a single-buyer business dependent on the Ministry of Defence

risks.note: MD&A: 'Challenges in meeting aggressive timelines for complex indigenous platforms, integration issues, and certification requirements', reinforced by the SWOT weakness 'Long gestation periods and complexities in project execution'. This is the risk that sits directly against the forward promises - a 24+ aircraft/year LCA Mk1A rate, expedited HTT-40 production, and the IMRH / LCA Mk2 / CATS / HLFT / UAV development pipeline. It is corroborated inside the accounts: the inventory turnover ratio fell during FY 2025-26 because of rising work-in-progress on LCA Mk1A, HTT-40, ALH, LCH, Su-30 and AL-31FP engines - i.e. capital is accumulating in unfinished programmes. Mitigation disclosed: additional assembly lines to de-risk execution (a 3rd LCA Mk1A line was established at Nasik) and capacity/infrastructure build-up.
risks.risk: Execution risk on complex indigenous programmes - timelines, integration and certification

risks.note: SWOT Threats name 'Collaborations of Indian Private Companies with Global OEMs and capability building by their entities' and 'Direct competition from foreign companies entering into Indian market and pricing pressures in international markets'; MD&A Risks repeats 'Competition from domestic and foreign players'. MD&A industry commentary itself records 'greater private sector participation in the defence ecosystem' as a key structural shift - so the same Atmanirbhar policy that expands HAL's addressable market also builds its future competitors. The Outlook section concedes 'increasing competition both from private sector and global players' as a challenge to the positive outlook.
risks.risk: Erosion of the nomination monopoly by private Indian players partnered with global OEMs, and by foreign entrants

risks.note: MD&A Risks: 'Rapid advancements leading to obsolescence of existing systems'; SWOT Threats: 'Rapid technological disruptions requiring continuous upgradation'; Outlook: 'evolving technological requirements'. The exposure is amplified by the nature of the installed base HAL supports - it describes itself as a 'trusted partner of Indian Defence Forces for providing support to aging fleets, some of which are more than 60 years old'. Mitigation disclosed: investment in R&D, advanced materials, advanced manufacturing technologies, automation, Industry 4.0, additive manufacturing, digitalisation and AI-enabled systems.
risks.risk: Technological obsolescence and the pace of upgrade required across a very long-lived fleet

risks.note: SWOT Threats: 'Supply chain disruptions due to geopolitical issues'; Outlook: 'supply chain constraints'. HAL's MiG Complex is built around production, MRO and upgrade of fixed-wing aircraft and engines 'mainly of Russian origin', and a financial-statement note records bulk contracts with the Russian Federation under which suppliers do not indicate itemised prices, so the value of materials issued has to be assessed on technical estimates and remains subject to adjustment at the end of the project - a disclosed weakness in price transparency on a geopolitically exposed supply line. Mitigations: supplier diversification, alternate indigenous sources, strategic inventories and closer coordination with global suppliers.
risks.risk: Supply-chain disruption from geopolitical events, including Russia-origin supply exposure

risks.note: The Board's Report states that due to non-appointment of the requisite number of Independent Directors, the Audit Committee and the Nomination & Remuneration Committee 'were not in valid constitution during the financial year till June 1, 2025', and that the CSR & Sustainable Development Committee, the Stakeholders Relationship Committee AND the Risk Management Committee were 'also not in valid constitution during the period from April 28, 2025 till June 1, 2025' - i.e. all five statutory committees, including the very committee that owns ESG, cyber security and business continuity risk, lapsed simultaneously for over a month. As on March 31, 2026 five Independent Director positions including the one woman Independent Director were still vacant against a sanctioned strength of seven. A disclosed consequence: related-party transactions requiring Audit Committee recommendation between April 1 and June 1, 2025 were put directly to the Board. HAL cannot self-remedy this - all directors are appointed by the President of India through the Administrative Ministry.
risks.risk: Governance capacity risk - Board and statutory committees ran part of the year without valid constitution

risks.note: SWOT weakness: 'Limited presence in high-value global export markets'. The BRSR quantifies it: exports contributed 1.58% of total turnover in FY 2025-26, to 13 countries during the year (30 countries over the Company's history). Expanding exports is one of HAL's stated principal strategies and the outlook leans on 'intensifying efforts to expand its global footprint', so the gap between the strategic weight placed on exports and their current contribution is itself the risk - domestic MoD demand remains effectively the only revenue engine, which loops back to the customer-concentration risk above.
risks.risk: Export weakness - exports are a rounding error in turnover despite being a stated strategic priority

risks.note: Flagged by management twice - as the first item under MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' ('Dependence on foreign OEMs for supply of critical components and Spares') and as the first SWOT weakness ('Dependency on foreign OEMs for critical materials and LRUs'). It is structural, not cyclical: the annual report's own materials-consumption disclosure shows imported raw materials, spare parts and components at 80% of total consumption in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 77%), i.e. import reliance INCREASED during the year even as indigenisation was the stated top strategy. Management also concedes 'engine supply issues observed in prior periods'. Mitigations disclosed: accelerated R&D, technology-transfer partnerships including higher localisation in engines, vendor development programmes, diversification of suppliers, development of alternate indigenous sources, strategic inventories for critical items, an MoU with MIDHANI for a strategic metal bank for critical raw materials, and a stated aim of 65-75%+ indigenisation for major platforms. [The 80%/77% figures are ratios from a financial-statement note that this extraction otherwise does not reproduce; no rupee amounts are carried.]

risks.risk: Customer concentration - the business is effectively a single-buyer business dependent on the Ministry of Defence
risks.note: MD&A lists 'Dependence on limited customers for new contracts' among major risks and states under SWOT Threats: 'Mainly dependent on MoD for the contracts. Any change in procurement policy / preference can adversely affect our ability to grow or maintain our sales, earnings and cash flow.' The BRSR confirms the Indian Air Force, Navy, Army and Coast Guard as primary customers. The same counterparty is also the controlling shareholder (President of India through MoD, 71.64%), so commercial and ownership concentration coincide. A specific named vector is a shift 'from nomination to competitive procurement' by regular customers, which would remove the single-tender/nomination basis on which much of HAL's work is placed.

risks.risk: Execution risk on complex indigenous programmes - timelines, integration and certification
risks.note: MD&A: 'Challenges in meeting aggressive timelines for complex indigenous platforms, integration issues, and certification requirements', reinforced by the SWOT weakness 'Long gestation periods and complexities in project execution'. This is the risk that sits directly against the forward promises - a 24+ aircraft/year LCA Mk1A rate, expedited HTT-40 production, and the IMRH / LCA Mk2 / CATS / HLFT / UAV development pipeline. It is corroborated inside the accounts: the inventory turnover ratio fell during FY 2025-26 because of rising work-in-progress on LCA Mk1A, HTT-40, ALH, LCH, Su-30 and AL-31FP engines - i.e. capital is accumulating in unfinished programmes. Mitigation disclosed: additional assembly lines to de-risk execution (a 3rd LCA Mk1A line was established at Nasik) and capacity/infrastructure build-up.

risks.risk: Erosion of the nomination monopoly by private Indian players partnered with global OEMs, and by foreign entrants
risks.note: SWOT Threats name 'Collaborations of Indian Private Companies with Global OEMs and capability building by their entities' and 'Direct competition from foreign companies entering into Indian market and pricing pressures in international markets'; MD&A Risks repeats 'Competition from domestic and foreign players'. MD&A industry commentary itself records 'greater private sector participation in the defence ecosystem' as a key structural shift - so the same Atmanirbhar policy that expands HAL's addressable market also builds its future competitors. The Outlook section concedes 'increasing competition both from private sector and global players' as a challenge to the positive outlook.

risks.risk: Technological obsolescence and the pace of upgrade required across a very long-lived fleet
risks.note: MD&A Risks: 'Rapid advancements leading to obsolescence of existing systems'; SWOT Threats: 'Rapid technological disruptions requiring continuous upgradation'; Outlook: 'evolving technological requirements'. The exposure is amplified by the nature of the installed base HAL supports - it describes itself as a 'trusted partner of Indian Defence Forces for providing support to aging fleets, some of which are more than 60 years old'. Mitigation disclosed: investment in R&D, advanced materials, advanced manufacturing technologies, automation, Industry 4.0, additive manufacturing, digitalisation and AI-enabled systems.

risks.risk: Supply-chain disruption from geopolitical events, including Russia-origin supply exposure
risks.note: SWOT Threats: 'Supply chain disruptions due to geopolitical issues'; Outlook: 'supply chain constraints'. HAL's MiG Complex is built around production, MRO and upgrade of fixed-wing aircraft and engines 'mainly of Russian origin', and a financial-statement note records bulk contracts with the Russian Federation under which suppliers do not indicate itemised prices, so the value of materials issued has to be assessed on technical estimates and remains subject to adjustment at the end of the project - a disclosed weakness in price transparency on a geopolitically exposed supply line. Mitigations: supplier diversification, alternate indigenous sources, strategic inventories and closer coordination with global suppliers.

risks.risk: Governance capacity risk - Board and statutory committees ran part of the year without valid constitution
risks.note: The Board's Report states that due to non-appointment of the requisite number of Independent Directors, the Audit Committee and the Nomination & Remuneration Committee 'were not in valid constitution during the financial year till June 1, 2025', and that the CSR & Sustainable Development Committee, the Stakeholders Relationship Committee AND the Risk Management Committee were 'also not in valid constitution during the period from April 28, 2025 till June 1, 2025' - i.e. all five statutory committees, including the very committee that owns ESG, cyber security and business continuity risk, lapsed simultaneously for over a month. As on March 31, 2026 five Independent Director positions including the one woman Independent Director were still vacant against a sanctioned strength of seven. A disclosed consequence: related-party transactions requiring Audit Committee recommendation between April 1 and June 1, 2025 were put directly to the Board. HAL cannot self-remedy this - all directors are appointed by the President of India through the Administrative Ministry.

risks.risk: Export weakness - exports are a rounding error in turnover despite being a stated strategic priority
risks.note: SWOT weakness: 'Limited presence in high-value global export markets'. The BRSR quantifies it: exports contributed 1.58% of total turnover in FY 2025-26, to 13 countries during the year (30 countries over the Company's history). Expanding exports is one of HAL's stated principal strategies and the outlook leans on 'intensifying efforts to expand its global footprint', so the gap between the strategic weight placed on exports and their current contribution is itself the risk - domestic MoD demand remains effectively the only revenue engine, which loops back to the customer-concentration risk above.

one-line thesis: HAL is a fully-booked defence OEM (INR2.55 lakh cr order book, ~7.7x FY26 sales) with a near-certain LCA Mk-1A delivery ramp gated on GE engine supply; FY27 hinges on engines arriving from Aug-2026 and 20 LCA + 20+ HTT-40 deliveries materialising — execution timing, not demand, is the only swing factor.

guidance (verify next quarter):
- **FY27 revenue: double-digit growth, "10-12% minimum"** (vs ~7% in FY26).
- **FY27 EBITDA margin: 30-31% maintained** (no margin compression despite manufacturing mix rise; ERV + material/labour escalation clauses in every contract, including ROH; inventory for FY27 already built so no cost spike).
- **LCA Mk-1A: ~20 deliveries targeted in FY27** (gated on GE engines — 6 received, ~15-20 more committed). Delivery start expected **Aug/Sep 2026**.
- **HTT-40: 20+ deliveries in FY27**, completion by ~FY30. Honeywell engine supply "stabilised," engines from next month.
- **Su-30 (12 a/c order): 1 in FY28, remaining 11 in FY29.**
- **Tejas Mk-II rollout: Q4FY26→ "by March" (next year-end)**; F414 engine order ~2 years out.
- **Mix shift: Mfg/ROH moving from ~30/70 toward 50/50** over coming years.
- **Order pipeline: ~INR90,000 cr (incl. ROH) over next 2 years.**
order book & pipeline:
- Order book INR2,54,538 cr (~7.7x FY26 revenue). Export order book ~INR400 cr; development order book ~INR3,000 cr.
- FY26 wins: 97 LCA Mk-1A (IAF); 6 ALH Mk-III MR (ICG); 8 Do-228 (ICG); 10 ALH Dhruv NG (Pawan Hans); 2 Hindustan-228 (Guyana).
- Pipeline at approval stages: **143 ALH (Army)** — flagged as the major contributor; Su-30 upgrade; upgrade of 40 Do-228; UH-M, 12 LUH LSP pending. ~INR90,000 cr over 2 yrs (incl. ROH ~INR20,000 cr/yr ≈ INR40-50k cr; balance new mfg).
- Su-30 upgrade is a **design program first (~5-6 yrs)**; CCS approval expected FY27, production only after design phase.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Manufacturing in execution:** LCA, 12 Su-30, AL-31FP engines (~32-35/yr target), Do-228, 21 ALH, LCH, HTT-40, RD-33 engines (only 15 left, all in FY27).
- **ROH/spares:** INR20,524 cr, broadly flat — no new platform added; spares down INR500-600 cr. LCA ROH cycle starts ~3 yrs after delivery (38 LCA already delivered from earlier contracts begin entering ROH). ROH priced cost-plus (PPRC mechanism), no fixed % of equipment value.
- Revenue recognition is **on delivery (not % completion)** → potential lumpiness when LCA/HTT-40 deliveries cluster.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Space:** SSLV Technology-Transfer Agreement (ISRO/IN-SPACe/NSIL, non-exclusive licence to manufacture SSLV); LVM3 / BlueBird Block-2 hardware supply.
- **Civil aerospace global supply chain:** Safran LEAP rotating parts (A320neo/737 MAX engines); SJ-100 commuter aircraft MoU with UAC Russia.
- **Indigenous engines:** Shakti civil engine DGCA certification; IMRH engine, GE F414 manufacturing infra planned.
- **UAVs:** rotary UAV prototype in ground test; CATS Warrior ground-run done, flight expected next year.
- **AMCA:** not currently in it; RFI is for D&D/prototype only — HAL hopeful of participating; production agency not yet decided. SU-57 = "government's call."
margins & cost dynamics:
- ~30% operating EBITDA margin held YoY; guided 30-31% for FY27.
- ROH margins slightly higher than manufacturing; mix shift to 50/50 mfg/ROH is mgmt's stated non-concern — "no stress on profitability."
- ERV (exchange-rate variation) clause in every contract incl. ROH; material & labour escalation factored in → claimed insulation from commodity/FX.
- FY27 inputs already in inventory (POs placed 1-2 yrs back for 83 LCA), so no near-term cost increase.
capex / expansion:
- FY26 capex INR2,386 cr; R&D INR2,794 cr.
- **~INR12,000 cr investment plan by 2030:** LCA Mk-II, GE F414 & IMRH engine infra, SSLV facilities, aero-engine indigenisation, D&D facilities.
- Capacity: 8 LCA Mk-1A/yr line at Nashik (3rd line, inaugurated Oct-2025); 3 LCA lines total (2 Bangalore + 1 Nashik); LCH at Bengaluru & Tumakuru focus.
- Strategy: HAL as core integrator — more outsourcing of full structures to private vendors + in-sourcing to keep manpower cost low; recruitment kept open (balanced).
capital allocation: - No dividend/buyback detail discussed on this call. Capital deployed into ~INR12,000 cr capacity build-out (to 2030) and heavy R&D (~8.4% of rev with capex). 24,000+ employees. PSU — govt is majority owner.
risks & watch-items:
- **GE engine dependency** — single biggest risk; deliveries repeatedly slipped (FY26 commitment of 2/month did not materialise). FY27 plan rests on ~20 engines arriving (1 in June, 2/month from Aug). Casting/supply-chain issues at GE Tier-2/3.
- **LCA software/testing refinements** — mgmt vague; analysts (JPMorgan) flagged investor anxiety that even FY27 deliveries are at risk. CMD repeatedly deflected specifics ("more technicalities").
- **Lumpy delivery-based revenue recognition** → quarterly volatility.
- **Manpower/private-sector competition** for skilled labour as 5-6 programs run in parallel (FY28-29).
- **Global supply-chain "slowness"** beyond GE (Honeywell now stabilised; radars/components).
- **GE penalty** for delayed engines — exists per contract but mgmt declined to quantify ("let delivery happen, then we'll see").
- **Uttam radar** integration controlled by DRDO — not in the 83-program; planned for the 97-program only.
management quality / tone: New CMD Ravi Kota (since 1 May 2026); measured, candid on supply chain but deliberately evasive on LCA technical/software specifics and GE penalty quantum. CFO Senapati precise on numbers and margin mechanics. Overall tone: confident-but-hedged ("plan B," "ways and means"); credibility partly hostage to whether the oft-slipped Aug/Sep LCA start finally holds.
non-obvious takeaways:
- Manufacturing already grew via ALH/AL-31FP/RD-33 — LCA is incremental upside, not the base; the "20 LCA" target may concentrate in H2FY27, risking spill into FY28.
- ~INR8,000-8,100 cr of inventory is locked in undelivered LCA (raw material + WIP); unbilled revenue is on already-delivered units stuck on documentation — a quiet working-capital / cash-conversion drag.
- ROH (the higher-margin, ~62% pool) is structurally flat until LCA/LCH enter overhaul (~3 yrs post-delivery) — near-term growth is lower-margin manufacturing-led.
- The 97 LCA order is what guarantees ~100% capacity utilisation across all 3 lines — backlog underwrites the capex.
- Safran LEAP + SJ-100 + SSLV = optionality to diversify beyond captive Indian-MoD demand into global civil/space supply chains.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: India's leading aerospace and defence Maharatna PSU, a Government Company in which the President of India acting through the Ministry of Defence holds 71.64% equity, engaged in design, development, manufacture, repair, overhaul, upgrade and servicing of aircraft, helicopters, aero-engines, …

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: HAL designs, develops, manufactures, repairs, overhauls, upgrades and services a wide range of products including aircraft, helicopters, aero-engines, avionics, accessories and aerospace structures. The Company was set up to meet the requirement of the Indian Defence Forces - the Indian Air Force, Indian Army, Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard - in the area of aerospace, and also supports civil and international customers. It relies on indigenous research as well as technology-transfer and licence agreements to manufacture its products, and its operations are organised into five complexes covering production, MRO, upgrade and R&D.

- **FY27 revenue: double-digit growth, "10-12% minimum"** (vs ~7% in FY26).
- **FY27 EBITDA margin: 30-31% maintained** (no margin compression despite manufacturing mix rise; ERV + material/labour escalation clauses in every contract, including ROH; inventory for FY27 already built so no cost spike).
- **LCA Mk-1A: ~20 deliveries targeted in FY27** (gated on GE engines — 6 received, ~15-20 more committed). Delivery start expected **Aug/Sep 2026**.
- **HTT-40: 20+ deliveries in FY27**, completion by ~FY30. Honeywell engine supply "stabilised," engines from next month.
- **Su-30 (12 a/c order): 1 in FY28, remaining 11 in FY29.**
- **Tejas Mk-II rollout: Q4FY26→ "by March" (next year-end)**; F414 engine order ~2 years out.
- **Mix shift: Mfg/ROH moving from ~30/70 toward 50/50** over coming years.
- **Order pipeline: ~INR90,000 cr (incl. ROH) over next 2 years.**

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- **Space:** SSLV Technology-Transfer Agreement (ISRO/IN-SPACe/NSIL, non-exclusive licence to manufacture SSLV); LVM3 / BlueBird Block-2 hardware supply.
- **Civil aerospace global supply chain:** Safran LEAP rotating parts (A320neo/737 MAX engines); SJ-100 commuter aircraft MoU with UAC Russia.
- **Indigenous engines:** Shakti civil engine DGCA certification; IMRH engine, GE F414 manufacturing infra planned.
- **UAVs:** rotary UAV prototype in ground test; CATS Warrior ground-run done, flight expected next year.
- **AMCA:** not currently in it; RFI is for D&D/prototype only — HAL hopeful of participating; production agency not yet decided. SU-57 = "government's call."

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The aerospace and defence sector is undergoing a significant structural shift driven by evolving geopolitical dynamics, rapid technological advancements and increasing emphasis on self-reliance, and witnessed sustained momentum during FY 2025-26
- Government focus on 'Atmanirbhar Bharat', indigenisation and modernisation of the Armed Forces supports demand
- Geopolitical uncertainties and the need to enhance operational readiness drove higher demand for indigenous platforms including fighter aircraft, helicopters, engines and related systems
- Structural shifts include greater private sector participation in the defence ecosystem, policy support through positive indigenisation lists, export promotion measures and infrastructure development for aerospace manufacturing
- The industry as a whole saw record-level order inflows and production ramp-ups in select segments
- Outlook for FY 2026-27 and beyond will remain positive, supported by a strong order book providing 7-8 years of revenue visibility
- Management expects improved growth through better supply chain stabilisation, capacity expansion (including significant infrastructure investments) and faster production ramp-up for key platforms
- Execution of ongoing programmes, coupled with anticipated new orders in fighter aircraft, rotary-wing platforms and upgrade projects, is expected to provide revenue visibility over the medium to long term
- Emerging opportunities in unmanned systems, advanced materials, digital manufacturing and space applications are expected to open new growth avenues
- Opportunity set cited: Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan and Positive Indigenisation List; Government focus on building an A&D ecosystem to cut the import bill and make India an A&D hub; civil MRO opportunities in India and expansion in MRO and lifecycle support services; new potential markets in India such as regional jets and UAVs
- Headwinds cited: evolving technological requirements, supply chain constraints, and increasing competition from both private sector and global players; pricing pressure in international markets; possible customer shift from nomination to competitive procurement; dependence on MoD for contracts
- Weaknesses cited: dependency on foreign OEMs for critical materials and LRUs, long gestation periods and complexity in project execution, and limited presence in high-value global export markets
- Mitigation stated: focus on enhancing operational efficiency, strengthening the supply chain ecosystem, accelerating indigenisation and investing in R&D is expected to mitigate these risks
- NOTE: no segment-wise or product-wise performance narrative is provided. MD&A item 5 states Government companies engaged in Defence Production are exempted from Ind AS 108 'Operating Segment' by MCA Notification No. 1/2/2014-CL-V dated February 23, 2018, with disclosure made at Clause 37 of Note 49. This is an explicitly stated absence.
- The Order Book position of the Company stands at Rs 2,54,53,848 Lakh as on March 31, 2026 (Board's Report, 'Order Book Position'). Source unit as printed: ` in Lakh.
- During FY 2025-26 the Company received manufacturing contracts of over Rs 69,60,000 Lakh and ROH (repair and overhaul) contracts of over Rs 17,30,000 Lakh
- Major orders bagged during the year: Qty 97 LCA Mk1A, Qty 06 ALH MkIII MR and Qty 8 Do-228 to the Indian Armed Forces; Qty 10 ALH Dhruv NG to M/s Pawan Hans Ltd; Qty 2 Hindustan-228 to Guyana
- MD&A SWOT lists 'Strong order book ensuring long-term revenue visibility' as a company strength
- MD&A Outlook: the order book provides 7-8 years of revenue visibility, and anticipated new orders in fighter aircraft, rotary-wing platforms and upgrade projects are expected to extend revenue visibility over the medium to long term
- MD&A industry commentary notes the industry as a whole saw record-level order inflows during FY 2025-26

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:
- ~30% operating EBITDA margin held YoY; guided 30-31% for FY27.
- ROH margins slightly higher than manufacturing; mix shift to 50/50 mfg/ROH is mgmt's stated non-concern — "no stress on profitability."
- ERV (exchange-rate variation) clause in every contract incl. ROH; material & labour escalation factored in → claimed insulation from commodity/FX.
- FY27 inputs already in inventory (POs placed 1-2 yrs back for 83 LCA), so no near-term cost increase.

capital_allocation.body: - No dividend/buyback detail discussed on this call. Capital deployed into ~INR12,000 cr capacity build-out (to 2030) and heavy R&D (~8.4% of rev with capex). 24,000+ employees. PSU — govt is majority owner.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: HAL's stated expansion posture for FY 2025-26 is capacity build-up in support of platform ramp-up rather than entry into new capacity classes. The Board's Report records capital expenditure incurred in FY 2025-26 channelised mainly towards the Green Field Helicopter Project at Tumakuru, augmentation of facilities for LCA, ROH (repair and overhaul) of Su-30, ROH of the AL-31FP engine and IT infrastructure, besides regular replacement and rationalisation of existing facilities on the infrastructure front; on the R&D front the spend went to the IMRH, CATS, UHM, Civil ALH and LUH projects. No commissioning, completion or ramp date is disclosed for any of these projects. The single completed physical expansion named for the year is a 3rd LCA Mk1A production line established at HAL Nasik to enhance LCA Mk1A production capacity. MD&A frames the forward plan as 'Expanding production capabilities to meet growing demand' and, under measures to tackle risks, as 'Capacity and Infrastructure Build-up: significant CAPEX investments in new production facilities, modernization of existing lines and establishment of additional assembly lines to de-risk execution'; the Outlook section attributes expected growth to better supply chain stabilisation, capacity expansion including significant infrastructure investments, and faster production ramp-up for key platforms, with a stated aim of 24+ LCA Mk1A aircraft annually in coming years and expedited HTT-40 production. Organisationally the footprint is 20 Divisions and 10 R&D Centres at ten geographic locations in seven states, grouped into five Complexes (Bangalore, MiG, Helicopter, Accessories, Design). Three supply-chain/industrial build-out agreements signed during the year are relevant to future capacity but reached this bundle only via the sibling strategy_outlook bundle (this bundle's Board's Report copy is truncated before them): an MoU with Yantra India Limited dated September 23, 2025 for funding the establishment of a 10,000 Ton extrusion press; an MoU with Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI) dated November 3, 2025 to set up a strategic metal bank for critical raw materials at MIDHANI; and an agreement with Safran Aircraft Engines dated June 19, 2025 for industrialisation and production of rotating parts for LEAP engines. On the land/asset side, Note 49 clause 14 discloses a large but partly encumbered land estate: Facilities Management Division holds 2,117.289 acres (2,096.189 acres freehold at Bangalore, 15.1 acres at Bagalkot, 6 acres leasehold at Harapanahalli), of which 17.737 acres is under litigation/encroachment by third parties and 10.152 acres is under dispute with BEML; titles to 30 survey numbers totalling 76.475 acres at FMD are not in the Company's name (Records of Tenancy Certificate available); Nasik division freehold land is 4,620.13 acres with 0.0516 acres encroached by 9 persons; about 50.21 acres at Koraput division is encroached by nearby villagers for cultivation; and title deeds are not in the Company's name for land acquired through Government grants in Uttar Pradesh (376.76 acres acquired by the State Government plus 54.30 acres transferred from the IAF in 1973, out of a total 431.06 acres of which 2.03 acres was sold to NHAI). A monetisation exercise for 2.925 acres at Okalipuram, Bengaluru is in process at a Reserve Price of Rs 9,780 lakhs after an earlier e-auction sale was annulled on 4th July 2023 following a Government Audit enquiry. Land has also been given on lease by Korwa Division (39.79 acres to Ordnance Factory Board, 0.115 acres to RCMA, 0.37 acres to AFLE, 3.08 acres to DAV College Trust) and 2.47 acres at Ojhar Nasik to MSRTC, and small parcels have been compulsorily acquired for the Bangalore metro rail project (0.078 acres at Benniganahalli; 711.22 sq m at the Corporate office, with compensation litigation pending before the City Civil Court and Writ Petition No. 640 of 2026 before the High Court). BRSR Principle 2 states that 0.48% of total capex in FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: 0.25%) was invested in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts - energy-efficient transformers, HVAC equipment, LED lighting and energy monitoring systems - while the equivalent share of R&D expenditure is explicitly 'Not tracked'.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: New CMD Ravi Kota (since 1 May 2026); measured, candid on supply chain but deliberately evasive on LCA technical/software specifics and GE penalty quantum. moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Integrated aerospace business spanning R&D, production and MRO including PBL solutions for fixed-wing aircraft, rotary-wing aircraft, aero-engines, LRUs and airborne systems (SWOT - Strengths)
- Strong order book ensuring long-term revenue visibility (SWOT - Strengths); management states the order book provides 7-8 years of revenue visibility
- Expertise in aircraft upgrade for Defence customers including re-engining, avionics upgrade and weapon system integration (SWOT - Strengths)
- Expertise in executing Transfer of Technology (ToT) projects - has absorbed ToT and produced MiG-21, MiG-27, Su-30MKI, Jaguar, Hawk, Dornier-228 and AVRO (SWOT - Strengths)
- Design and development expertise across a wide helicopter range - ALH variants, LCH, LUH in the 3.5-to-5.5-ton class, civil ALH Dhruv-NG, and IMRH/DBMRH under development in the 10-15-ton class (SWOT - Strengths)
- Trusted partner of the Indian Defence Forces for supporting ageing fleets, some more than 60 years old (SWOT - Strengths)
- Government ownership and Maharatna PSU status - President of India through MoD holds 71.64% equity
- Policy tailwind: Atmanirbhar Bharat, Positive Indigenisation List and export promotion measures cited as opportunities

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **GE engine dependency** — single biggest risk; deliveries repeatedly slipped (FY26 commitment of 2/month did not materialise). FY27 plan rests on ~20 engines arriving (1 in June, 2/month from Aug). Casting/supply-chain issues at GE Tier-2/3.
- **LCA software/testing refinements** — mgmt vague; analysts (JPMorgan) flagged investor anxiety that even FY27 deliveries are at risk. CMD repeatedly deflected specifics ("more technicalities").
- **Lumpy delivery-based revenue recognition** → quarterly volatility.
- **Manpower/private-sector competition** for skilled labour as 5-6 programs run in parallel (FY28-29).
- **Global supply-chain "slowness"** beyond GE (Honeywell now stabilised; radars/components).
- **GE penalty** for delayed engines — exists per contract but mgmt declined to quantify ("let delivery happen, then we'll see").
- **Uttam radar** integration controlled by DRDO — not in the 83-program; planned for the 97-program only.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- Manufacturing already grew via ALH/AL-31FP/RD-33 — LCA is incremental upside, not the base; the "20 LCA" target may concentrate in H2FY27, risking spill into FY28.
- ~INR8,000-8,100 cr of inventory is locked in undelivered LCA (raw material + WIP); unbilled revenue is on already-delivered units stuck on documentation — a quiet working-capital / cash-conversion drag.
- ROH (the higher-margin, ~62% pool) is structurally flat until LCA/LCH enter overhaul (~3 yrs post-delivery) — near-term growth is lower-margin manufacturing-led.
- The 97 LCA order is what guarantees ~100% capacity utilisation across all 3 lines — backlog underwrites the capex.
- Safran LEAP + SJ-100 + SSLV = optionality to diversify beyond captive Indian-MoD demand into global civil/space supply chains.

themes.title: Defence indigenization & order-book visibility
themes.need: Indigenization mandates (IDDM / Atmanirbhar / DcPP) plus multi-year order books make domestic defence the cleanest revenue-conversion theme - across electronics, drones, simulators, explosives/munitions and precision systems. BEL guides >INR55k cr FY27 inflow (~INR30k cr QRSAM pending CCS clearance, guided by September) on a INR72,258cr order book; HAL book ~INR2.55 lakh cr; SOLARINDS defence revenue +94% to INR2,634cr FY26, guided >INR4,500cr FY27 on an ~INR18,000cr defence order book (Bhargavastra counter-drone trials completing CY2026); DATAPATTNS inflows strong; BHARATFORG/BEML add land-systems and platforms.
themes.driver: Backlog-to-revenue conversion underway; BEL's QRSAM CCS clearance (guided by Sep-2026, ~INR30k cr of the FY27 inflow guide) is the load-bearing near-term catalyst; fresh MoD orders + emergency procurement; HAL LCA Mk-1A ramp (gated on GE engines).

themes.title: Commercial-aerospace supply chain (Boeing/Airbus/engine OEMs)
themes.need: A record global commercial-aircraft backlog plus engine-OEM (GE/Safran/Honeywell/RR/P&W) outsourcing and China+1 are pulling Indian build-to-print suppliers up the value chain - aero-engine hot-section airfoils, airframe structures, tooling and wire harnesses. AZAD ramping engine/airfoil exports; UNIMECH near-tripling tooling capacity; AEQUS/SANSERA on precision aero; ROSSTECH on harnesses; PTCIL on titanium castings.
themes.driver: New commercial-aero RFP wins; engine-component capacity ramps; new MRO licences; Boeing/Airbus build-rate recovery.
